paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 June 2025 Q12(b)

parts.question_text: Light from the Sun is unpolarised. Explain the difference between unpolarised light and plane polarised light.
mark_scheme: Unpolarised light has oscillations / vibrations in all / many planes (or directions).
Plane polarised light has oscillations / vibrations in one plane (or direction).
The plane includes the direction of wave travel (or: the direction of oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of wave travel). [MP3 dependent on MP2]
parts.sample_answer: Unpolarised light has oscillations in many different planes, whereas plane polarised light has oscillations in only one plane. This single plane contains the direction in which the wave travels – equivalently, the oscillations are in one direction perpendicular to the direction of travel.

parts.question_text: A student uses a polarising filter to view light reflected from a glass block. Explain what she would observe as she rotates the filter through 360°.
mark_scheme: The intensity (brightness) of the light varies.
From a maximum to a minimum every 90° of rotation.
Maximum intensity occurs when the (plane of the) polarising filter is in the same direction as the plane of oscillation of the light (or minimum when they are perpendicular).
parts.sample_answer: The brightness of the reflected light changes as the filter is rotated, going from a maximum to a minimum every 90°. The light is brightest when the filter's plane of polarisation is aligned with the plane of oscillation of the (partially polarised) reflected light, and dimmest when the two are perpendicular.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 Jan 2025 Q18

parts.question_text: A student directs unpolarised light through a polarising filter. After passing through the polarising filter, the light is plane polarised. Explain the difference between unpolarised light and plane polarised light.
mark_scheme: Unpolarised light has oscillations / vibrations in all / many planes (or directions).
Plane polarised light has oscillations / vibrations in one plane (or direction).
Which includes the direction of wave travel (or: which is perpendicular to the direction of wave travel). [MP3 dependent on MP1 and MP2]
parts.sample_answer: Unpolarised light oscillates in all possible planes; plane polarised light oscillates in a single plane, which contains the direction of travel of the wave (the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel).

parts.question_text: The student rotates the polarising filter. Explain why rotating the polarising filter will not change the intensity of the light that passes through the filter.
mark_scheme: The polarising filter only transmits light (oscillating) in one plane / direction.
As the filter is rotated, a different single plane / direction of oscillation passes through, so the intensity stays the same.
parts.sample_answer: The filter only transmits oscillations in one plane. Because unpolarised light contains oscillations in every plane equally, whichever way the filter is turned it transmits one plane's worth of oscillations, so the transmitted intensity is unchanged.

parts.question_text:
The student arranges three polarising filters in series. Initially filter 1 and filter 2 have the same (vertical) plane of polarisation and filter 3 is horizontal, at 90° to filter 2. The student rotates filter 2 by 45°. The intensity of light that passes through filter 3 changes.
Explain how rotating filter 2 by 45° from its initial orientation affects the intensity of light passing through filter 3.
mark_scheme: Initial orientation: filter 1 is aligned with filter 2, so light is transmitted through filter 2 (filter 2 transmits the light transmitted by filter 1).
Filter 3 is perpendicular to filter 2,
so no light passes through filter 3.
After rotation: some light transmitted through filter 2 is also transmitted through filter 3.
So the intensity of light transmitted through filter 3 increases.
parts.sample_answer: Initially filter 1 and filter 2 are aligned, so the plane polarised light from filter 1 passes through filter 2. Filter 3 is perpendicular to filter 2, so none of that light passes through filter 3 and the intensity after filter 3 is zero. When filter 2 is rotated by 45°, the light leaving filter 2 is now polarised at 45°, which is no longer perpendicular to filter 3, so some of it is transmitted through filter 3. The intensity of light passing through filter 3 therefore increases from zero.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 Jan 2026 Q18(c)

parts.question_text: Radio waves from a transmitter are detected by a vertical aerial. When the teacher rotated the aerial by 90° so that it was horizontal, the radio waves were no longer detected. Explain this observation.
mark_scheme: The oscillations of the radio waves are in one plane / direction only, i.e. the radio waves are plane polarised.
The horizontal aerial cannot absorb / detect waves whose oscillations are in the vertical plane.
parts.sample_answer: The radio waves are plane polarised, with their oscillations in the vertical plane. A horizontal aerial cannot absorb oscillations that are perpendicular to it, so when the aerial is turned horizontal no signal is detected.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 past paper (Diffraction & Polarisation topic pack Q1(b)(ii))

parts.question_text: Light from the Sun arriving at a panel of solar cells is unpolarised. Describe how a student can demonstrate that light from the Sun is unpolarised.
mark_scheme: Direct the light through a polarising filter (and rotate the filter).
There is no change in intensity as the filter is rotated (or: if it were polarised, the intensity would change as the filter is rotated).
parts.sample_answer: View the sunlight through a single polarising filter and rotate the filter. If the light is unpolarised, the brightness of the transmitted light does not change as the filter is rotated; polarised light would show a change in intensity.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 past paper (Diffraction & Polarisation topic pack Q2(a))

parts.question_text: A teacher has a laser pointer. The laser pointer emits a narrow beam of plane polarised light. Describe how the teacher can demonstrate that the light from the laser pointer is plane polarised.
mark_scheme: Direct the light through one polarising filter.
Rotate the filter until no light passes through (or: rotate the filter and the light changes intensity).
parts.sample_answer: Shine the laser beam through a single polarising filter and rotate the filter. Because the light is plane polarised, the transmitted intensity changes as the filter rotates and falls to zero when the filter's plane of polarisation is perpendicular to that of the light.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 past paper (Diffraction & Polarisation topic pack Q3)

parts.question_text:
A student wearing polarising sunglasses observes a mobile phone screen. The student rotates the mobile phone through 90°. The screen then appears completely black.
Explain why the screen appears completely black when the student rotates the mobile phone through 90°.
mark_scheme: Light emitted from the mobile phone screen is (plane) polarised.
When the phone is rotated, the plane of polarisation of the light and the plane of polarisation of the polarising filter in the sunglasses are perpendicular.
So the sunglasses / polarising filter absorb the light.
parts.sample_answer: The light from the phone screen is plane polarised. Rotating the phone through 90° makes the plane of polarisation of the screen's light perpendicular to the plane of polarisation of the filters in the sunglasses, so the filters absorb all of the light and the screen looks black.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 past paper (Diffraction & Polarisation topic pack Q4(c))

parts.question_text:
Polarisation can be used to identify when some materials are under stress. Placing the material under stress causes the plane of polarisation of the light passing through the material to be rotated. The greater the stress, the greater the rotation of the plane of polarisation of the light.
A piece of transparent material under stress is positioned between two polarising filters. There is an angle of 90° between the planes of polarisation of the two polarising filters. A photograph taken through the second filter shows bright and dark regions.
Explain how this photograph can be used to identify areas of the material with different amounts of stress.
mark_scheme: (Polarising) filters at 90° to each other do not allow light to pass through.
Rotation of the plane of polarisation (due to stress) allows light to pass.
Darker areas represent less stress (or brighter areas represent greater stress).
parts.sample_answer: With the two filters crossed at 90°, no light would normally get through. Where the material is stressed it rotates the plane of polarisation of the light, so some light is no longer perpendicular to the second filter and is transmitted. Brighter regions in the photograph therefore correspond to greater stress and darker regions to less stress.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 Oct 2019 Q18

parts.question_text:
When an incident ray of light meets a boundary between air and glass, some of the light is reflected and some is refracted. The reflected light is partially plane polarised.
State what is meant by plane polarised.
mark_scheme: Vibrations / oscillations (of the wave) in one plane (only).
The plane includes the direction of wave travel (or: the vibrations are in one direction perpendicular to the direction of wave travel).
parts.sample_answer: Plane polarised light has its vibrations (oscillations) in one plane only. That plane contains the direction in which the wave travels — equivalently, the oscillations are all in one direction perpendicular to the direction of travel.

parts.question_text: Deduce whether the refracted ray is unpolarised or partially plane polarised.
mark_scheme: The refracted ray lacks the planes of oscillation that are in the reflected light (or: the refracted ray has a plane of polarisation perpendicular to the plane of polarisation of the reflected light).
So the refracted ray must also be partially plane polarised. [MP2 dependent on MP1]
parts.sample_answer: The reflected light is partially plane polarised, so it contains more of one plane of oscillation than the others. The refracted ray carries the rest of the light, so it lacks those planes of oscillation (its plane of polarisation is perpendicular to that of the reflected light). The refracted ray must therefore also be partially plane polarised.

parts.question_text:
At the Brewster angle θB, the reflected light is completely plane polarised. This occurs when the reflected ray and the refracted ray are at right angles to each other, so θB + r = 90°.
Show that tan θB = ng / na, where na is the refractive index of air and ng is the refractive index of glass.
mark_scheme: Use of na sin θa = ng sin θg (or: na sin θB = ng sin r).
Substitute r = 90° − θB, giving na sin θB = ng sin(90° − θB) = ng cos θB (or: sin r = cos θB).
Divide sin θB by cos θB to give tan θB, leading to tan θB = ng / na.
parts.sample_answer: Snell's law at the air–glass boundary gives na sin θB = ng sin r. At the Brewster angle the reflected and refracted rays are at right angles, so r = 90° − θB and na sin θB = ng sin(90° − θB) = ng cos θB. Dividing both sides by cos θB gives na tan θB = ng, so tan θB = ng / na.

parts.question_text:
Calculate θB for light passing from air into glass.
refractive index of air = 1.00
refractive index of glass = 1.50
mark_scheme: Substitution of values into tan θB = ng / na (tan θB = 1.50 / 1.00).

parts.question_text:
Different colours of visible light are refracted as they pass through a prism: violet light is refracted the most and red light the least.
A student suggests that the Brewster angle for violet light would be smaller than that for red light, as violet is refracted more than red.
Criticise this suggestion.
mark_scheme: The refractive index (of the glass) is greater for violet than for red (or: ng / na is greater for violet).
Clearly links this to the student being incorrect: since tan θB = ng / na, a greater refractive index gives a greater θB, so the Brewster angle for violet is larger than for red.
parts.sample_answer: The student is incorrect. Since tan θB = ng / na, a colour with a larger refractive index has a larger Brewster angle. Violet is refracted more than red, so the refractive index of the glass is greater for violet; therefore tan θB — and hence θB — is greater for violet than for red, not smaller.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 Jan 2022 Q16(c)

parts.question_text:
The light emerging from prism B is observed through a polarising filter. The polarising filter is rotated gradually, and the light transmitted by the filter varies in intensity.
Explain how this observation demonstrates that light waves are transverse.
mark_scheme: The light (emerging from prism B) is polarised (its intensity changes as the polarising filter is rotated).
Only transverse waves can be polarised.
parts.sample_answer: As the polarising filter is rotated the transmitted intensity varies, which shows that the emerging light is (plane) polarised. Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel (a longitudinal wave cannot be polarised). Light must therefore be a transverse wave.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 past paper multiple choice (Diffraction & Polarisation topic pack)

parts.question_text:
A filament lamp is a source of unpolarised light. A polarising filter is placed between a filament lamp and an observer. The filter is rotated in the plane perpendicular to the direction of travel of the light.
Which of the following is observed as the filter is rotated through an angle of 90°?
A. The light intensity changes from maximum to minimum.
B. The light intensity changes from minimum to maximum.
C. The light intensity does not change.
D. The light intensity is zero throughout the rotation.
mark_scheme: Correct answer: C. The intensity transmitted by a single polarising filter from an unpolarised source does not vary as the filter is rotated.
parts.sample_answer: C

parts.question_text:
Which of the following describes the oscillations in polarised waves?
A. In a single plane which is perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
B. In many planes, which include the direction of wave travel
C. In many directions and parallel to the direction of wave travel
D. In one direction and perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
mark_scheme: Correct answer: D. Polarised waves have oscillations in one direction, perpendicular to the direction of wave travel. (A is wrong because the single plane of polarisation includes the direction of travel; it is not perpendicular to it.)
parts.sample_answer: D

parts.question_text:
Which of the following statements about waves is correct?
A. Both longitudinal and transverse waves can be polarised.
B. Neither longitudinal nor transverse waves can be polarised.
C. Only longitudinal waves can be polarised.
D. Only transverse waves can be polarised.
mark_scheme: Correct answer: D. Only transverse waves can be polarised.
parts.sample_answer: D

parts.question_text:
Which of the following can not be demonstrated in experiments using sound waves?
A. diffraction
B. polarisation
C. refraction
D. superposition
mark_scheme: Correct answer: B. Polarisation only occurs in transverse waves; sound is longitudinal. Diffraction, refraction and superposition can be demonstrated for all waves.
parts.sample_answer: B

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 June 2025 Q19

parts.question_text:
A scientist used a photocell to investigate the photoelectric effect. A photocell consists of a metal plate and an electrode. A beam of monochromatic light is directed onto the metal plate and causes the photoelectric effect. All photons in the beam have the same energy.
Explain why the beam produces photoelectrons with a range of kinetic energies.
mark_scheme: Each photon (absorbed) transfers all of its energy to one electron.
The energy is shared between the kinetic energy of the electron and the energy needed to break free.
Electrons need different amounts of energy to escape the surface (so the kinetic energy of the photoelectrons varies).
parts.sample_answer: Each photon gives all of its energy to a single electron. Part of that energy is used by the electron to escape from the metal and the rest becomes its kinetic energy. Electrons at the surface need only the work function to escape, but electrons deeper in the metal need more energy to reach the surface, so the photoelectrons emerge with a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum.

parts.question_text:
The scientist connected the photocell to an ammeter and battery. Photoelectrons are attracted to the electrode, causing a current in the circuit. The scientist directed different frequencies and intensities of light onto the photocell and made the following observations:
• white light with a low intensity caused no current
• white light with a high intensity caused no current
• ultraviolet light with a low intensity caused a current.
Explain what these observations show about the nature of light.
mark_scheme: In the wave model, more intense light has greater amplitude waves (or each wave transfers more energy).
(So) in the wave model light of any intensity would (eventually) release photoelectrons.
(In the particle model) intensity affects the number of photons per second, not the energy of each photon.
(But) ultraviolet photons have more energy than visible-light photons, so ultraviolet would cause the release of photoelectrons.
(So) this demonstrates the particle nature of light.
parts.sample_answer: If light were a wave, increasing the intensity would increase the energy delivered, so high-intensity white light should release electrons – yet it produces no current. In the photon model each photon's energy depends only on frequency (E = hf), and intensity only changes the number of photons per second. White-light photons do not have enough energy to overcome the work function however many there are, while higher-frequency ultraviolet photons do, even at low intensity. The observations therefore show that light behaves as particles (photons).

parts.question_text:
The scientist reversed the connections to the battery (the battery has negligible internal resistance), so that a potential difference of 1.5 V now opposes the photoelectrons. When photoelectrons have enough kinetic energy to overcome the potential difference across the photocell, there is a current in the circuit.
Ultraviolet light of wavelength 250 nm is incident on the photocell. Deduce whether there is a current in the circuit.
work function of metal plate in photocell = 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
mark_scheme: Use of E = hf (E = 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).
Use of hf = Φ + Ek,max (Ek,max = 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).
Converts from J to eV, or use of V = W/Q to find the energy needed (2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).
Ek,max = 0.66 eV < 1.5 eV (or 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J < 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) so no current is detected.
parts.sample_answer: f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 250 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.20 × 10¹⁵ Hz, so photon energy E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.20 × 10¹⁵ = 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Ek,max = hf − Φ = 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 0.66 eV. The opposing p.d. of 1.5 V requires 1.5 eV (2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). Since 0.66 eV < 1.5 eV, the photoelectrons cannot reach the electrode and there is no current.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 Jan 2026 Q21

parts.question_text:
A camera detects light using a charge-coupled device (CCD). One CCD has an array of metal pixels. The pixels release electrons when exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light. The pixels are exposed to UV light of wavelength 380 nm.
Show that the energy of a photon of this light is about 5.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
mark_scheme: Use of E = hf.
E = 5.23 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (given to at least 3 s.f.).

parts.question_text:
The manufacturer states that about 80% of these photons incident on a pixel will cause the emission of an electron.
Deduce whether the manufacturer's statement is accurate.
intensity of incident light = 1.1 μW m⁻²
diameter of pixel = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m
number of electrons emitted by each pixel per second = 195
mark_scheme: Calculates area of pixel (A = π(1.2 × 10⁻⁵)²/4 = 1.13 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²).
Calculates number of photons incident each second (1.24 × 10⁻¹⁶ / 5.23 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 238 s⁻¹).
Percentage of photons that release an electron = 195/238 = 82%.
82% ≈ 80% so the statement is accurate (or calculated percentage compared to 80% with a consistent conclusion).
parts.sample_answer: Pixel area A = π × (1.2 × 10⁻⁵)² / 4 = 1.13 × 10⁻¹⁰ m². Power on pixel P = IA = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.13 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 1.24 × 10⁻¹⁶ W. Photons per second = 1.24 × 10⁻¹⁶ / 5.23 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 238. Percentage releasing an electron = 195/238 × 100 = 82%, which is approximately 80%, so the manufacturer's statement is accurate.

parts.question_text:
The threshold frequency of the metal in the pixels is equal to the frequency of green light. The pixels were exposed to white light with the same intensity as the UV light. The UV light source was removed.
Explain how this changed the percentage of photons that released electrons.
mark_scheme: There is a range of frequencies / wavelengths (colours) in white light.
Only some frequencies will be higher than the threshold frequency.
Only some photons will have enough energy to release an electron (or energy greater than the work function).
So only a smaller percentage of photons would release electrons.
parts.sample_answer: White light contains a range of frequencies. Only the frequencies at or above the threshold frequency (green and higher: blue, violet) have photon energies greater than the work function; red, orange and yellow photons do not. So only some of the incident photons can release an electron and the percentage of photons releasing electrons decreases.

paper_source: Edexcel IAL WPH12 June 2025 Q15

parts.question_text:
Apparatus is used to demonstrate the diffraction of an electron beam in a school laboratory. A beam of electrons is accelerated by a high potential difference towards a piece of graphite. The graphite diffracts the electron beam, producing a diffraction pattern on the fluorescent screen.
State what is meant by diffraction.
mark_scheme: (Diffraction is) the spreading out of waves
when passing through a gap (slit) or around an object.
parts.sample_answer: Diffraction is the spreading out of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle.

parts.question_text: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 4.9 kV. Show that the de Broglie wavelength for the electron is about 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
mark_scheme: Use of Ek = ½mv² (v = 4.15 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹).
Use of λ = h/p.

parts.question_text:
A student suggests that the beam of electrons would produce a diffraction pattern if a diffraction grating with 5000 lines per cm was used. Deduce whether a second order maximum would be clearly visible on a screen placed about a metre away from the grating.
λ = 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ m
mark_scheme: Converts 5000 lines per cm to slit separation in m (d = 10⁻² / 5000 = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m).
Use of nλ = d sin θ (sin θ = 2 × 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ / 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵).
θ = 0.001° – this angle is very small, so the maximum would not be clearly visible.
parts.sample_answer: d = 1 cm / 5000 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. For n = 2: sin θ = 2 × 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ / 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, so θ ≈ 0.001°. This angle is far too small to separate the second order maximum from the central maximum on a screen a metre away, so it would not be clearly visible.
